The title lockup is fairly expected fantasy-epic chrome type with a sunburst.
The palette is safe and genre-standard compared with D's graphic reduction.

tells: The typography is the subject and has a real point of view. Latin glyphs are cut into fragments that rhyme with katakana (TOKYO set as hybrid forms), there are stencil letterforms, a dot-matrix pixel grid and scattered letter fields.

Every frame uses a different layout system: a bold cropped D with a target motif, a tracked letterspaced S G on a cyan bar, a framed glyph field, a diagonal slash with flying glyphs, an LED matrix and a dense collage. This is not a one-layout slideshow.
The palette is deliberate and unusual: hot pink, cyan, acid lime, violet and red on near-black, with paper grain and print-misregistration texture.
The frames build in density toward a layered finale, which implies choreography and escalation.
gaps: The idea leans on a familiar Tokyo, neon and glitch-typography idiom. It needs a more specific concept than 'city as signage' to match B's world-building device.
There is little real light or material depth. A physical or optical layer such as print, LED or projection could ground the flat graphics.
Some frames, like the LED grid, read as effect-led texture. The type should carry the message more legibly at key beats.

tells: The idea is a single memorable metaphor: an ad man's silhouette falls past skyscrapers papered with period advertising and lands nonchalantly on the sofa. That is the whole show in one gesture, a loop of collapse and composure.

Flat black cut-out silhouettes are set against desaturated period photography and ad collage. The compositions have bold scale contrast, like the giant shoe and the small falling figure against a vast tower, and every frame works as a poster.
Red and black two-weight credits in a mid-century grotesk sit as a disciplined system tied to the period.
The palette is restrained, with off-white, black, and red as the only accent, which is earned and echoed in the ad imagery.
The choreography is clear: enter the office, the floor dissolves, the fall rotates through space and the figure resolves into the iconic seated pose.
gaps: The credit typography is functional rather than expressive, and less ambitious than C's custom letterform work.
Its material and light are more graphic and flat than B's tactile, dimensional craft.
The flat cut-out silhouette style has been widely imitated since, so the frames read as more familiar today.

defects: Wing motion blur is faked with stacked echo copies, so you see 4-6 hard-edged ghost duplicates instead of a smooth smear. It reads as a cheap time-echo effect, not shutter blur.
The wings are flat, rigid cardboard paddles that hinge from one point. There is no feather breakup, no wing bend and no follow-through at the tips, so the hover has no weight or air.
The bird's body is a flat, dark silhouette with a pasted-on eye and beak. The rim light is just a thin bright outline with no real falloff into the form.
At 100% the whole frame is covered in heavy, uniform RGB noise. It looks like grain added to hide banding, and it turns the large gradients to mush instead of giving them texture.
Bokeh dust specks are evenly spaced, the same size and static, like an overlay layer, with no depth or parallax.
The wordmark's cast shadow is doubled and smeared. It reads as a copy offset onto the grass, not a shadow from any consistent light.
The end is dead: the last ~2 s are almost identical frames of the lockup with only grass shimmer.
The sky gradient and horizon are generic, with no atmospheric haze layering. The cut from close-up to wide shot jumps scale without any match on action.
gaps: Motion: the hover cycle is a mechanical flap loop that never varies, and the key story beat (the kestrel stooping and becoming the full stop) happens in a few frames with no anticipation, acceleration or impact/settle on the period. The idea's payoff is thrown away, then followed by ~2 s of static hold.

Sound: wing beats are identical gated noise bursts on a fixed grid, the dive is one filtered-noise swell, and the bird call is three thin sine chirps over a static low drone. There is no produced music, no low-end weight on the landing, and no tail or mix space. It is functional sync, but it sounds like synthesized placeholder sound.

Finish: crude echo-stack blur, rigid paddle wings and a blanket noise overlay instead of real shading, volumetric light and feather detail. Next to studio work the creature and the light both look unfinished, and the frames don't hold up as posters.
